messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Amina is an 80-year-old African American pastor who came to treatment only after months of pressure from her husband and one of the deacons at her church, both of whom had watched her world grow smaller. Decades earlier, before coming to the United States as a refugee, she had been seized during political violence in her home country. She still speaks of that time in fragments. She remembers being forced onto a crowded bus under guard, the metallic clatter of rifles against the bus frame, the sharp commands and cries around her, and the sensation that she was no longer a person with a name but something moved and handled at other people’s will. What has stayed with her most is not a coherent story but flashes: the sound of men shouting, the scrape of a weapon, bodies jerking when someone made a sudden move. Even now, when she tries to place the memory in the past, it can feel so extreme that she struggles to believe it truly happened to her.

In the years since, the ordinary settings of her life as a pastor have repeatedly touched those same raw points. Riding the city bus to visit parishioners is especially difficult. The lurch of the vehicle, strangers shifting suddenly in the aisle, and the feeling of being enclosed with no easy exit can make her feel unreal, as if she is no longer fully in her body. Seeing a weapon on a police officer’s belt, or even an object held in a way that could be used as a weapon, can stop her in place. In those moments she becomes immediately guarded, watching people’s hands and shoulders for any abrupt movement and checking behind her to make sure no one is following. She has come to believe that these reactions prove how unsafe the world remains, and each time they happen she is thrown back into the conviction that what was done to her was profoundly unjust and never answered for.

That sense of injustice sits alongside a more private conviction that if she lets herself think too directly about what happened, she will not be able to bear it. Because of that, she has spent years refusing to speak of the event, even with her husband. When church members ask why she no longer takes the bus across town, she gives practical excuses. She has also developed the habit of dressing in loose, concealing clothing, telling herself she does not want to be noticed. In the hospital clinic she missed two follow-up appointments after becoming distressed in the waiting room, and until now she has avoided psychological care altogether. These choices make sense to her: if she stays covered, says little, and does not put herself in situations that stir things up, she might keep herself together.

Instead, the silence has left the memory with a life of its own. Because she never tells the story through, it forces itself into her mind uninvited, often as sound before image. On the bus she may suddenly hear the shouted commands from years ago as if they are occurring again inside her head. At home, if her husband moves quickly behind her in the kitchen, she startles, scans the room, and a burst of the old scene comes back without warning. The more she stays on guard—eyes on other people, attention fixed on possible danger, repeatedly looking over her shoulder—the more easily the memory breaks through. And when it does, it confirms for her that she is still marked by what happened, still reduced in some fundamental way, “like an object, not a person,” as she once said haltingly.

That belief has increasingly shaped where she goes and how she works. As a pastor, she used to travel across the city for hospital visits, prayer meetings, and funerals. Now she rearranges her duties to avoid buses whenever possible, asks others to accompany her, and positions herself near doors during church gatherings. If someone in the congregation makes a sudden movement during a crowded service, she can feel herself go rigid, watching the room instead of listening to the prayer she is meant to lead. Afterwards she is ashamed and angry—angry that the original wrong was never righted, and ashamed that she still feels governed by it. Those thoughts make the next trigger sharper: the detached feeling is enough to frighten her on its own, because she has begun to read it as a sign that she is losing her grip and will not cope if the memory comes fully.

What finally brought Amina in was an incident on a bus she had taken despite herself to visit a sick church elder. A passenger swung a long umbrella while turning, and for an instant it looked like a weapon. She froze, heard shouting in her head, and felt the whole scene become unreal. She got off several stops early and called her husband in tears, something she had never done. She says she is seeking help now because she is afraid that if she continues living this way she will stop being able to serve her church and stop recognizing herself. At the same time, what frightens her most is that speaking about the past may make it all come back with more force than she can survive.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to threat and memories, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers directly lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette includes negative appraisals that shape future reactions, but it does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that those appraisals make triggers more likely or more salient.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Although threat and negative appraisals co-occur, no paragraph clearly states that a sense of threat itself leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes avoidance and safety behaviours alongside later triggering situations, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase or generate triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Seeing a weapon on a police officer’s belt, or even an object held in a way that could be used as a weapon, can stop her in place. In those moments she becomes immediately guarded, watching people’s hands and shoulders for any abrupt movement and checking behind her to make sure no one is following.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Just as quickly, the old conclusion settles over her that the world is still fundamentally unsafe and that she herself is still living at other people’s mercy, never fully restored to ordinary human security.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
And when it does, it confirms for her that she is still marked by what happened, still reduced in some fundamental way, “like an object, not a person,” as she once said haltingly.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once she has reached that bleak certainty, ordinary details snag more easily on her attention: a crowded aisle, a stranger turning too fast, the outline of something at a person’s hip all stand out at once as possible signs that danger is near.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In those moments she becomes immediately guarded, watching people’s hands and shoulders for any abrupt movement and checking behind her to make sure no one is following. She has come to believe that these reactions prove how unsafe the world remains, and each time they happen she is thrown back into the conviction that what was done to her was profoundly unjust and never answered for.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this endangered so suddenly has become, in her own mind, evidence that her life was permanently altered by the violence and that safety is something other people get to take for granted, not her.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In the hospital clinic she missed two follow-up appointments after becoming distressed in the waiting room, and until now she has avoided psychological care altogether. These choices make sense to her: if she stays covered, says little, and does not put herself in situations that stir things up, she might keep herself together.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But over time the very routes she no longer takes and the places she now approaches warily have become reminders in their own right; the bus stop she avoids, the clinic waiting room she dreads, even the need to scan for exits before a church gathering now cue the same anticipatory jolt before anything has actually happened.
<<<END>>>
